 A breakout product can quickly become a liability when growing sales expose defects that were once rare or difficult to detect. Research on millions of vehicle sales and recalls over a decade ... more Leer en español Ler em português Post

 Every executive wants a breakout product. What many forget, however, is that once a product becomes a hit, a new set of challenges emerges. As more customers use it, in more situations, more often, rare defects that barely registered in testing begin to surface. Complaints multiply, and regulators and journalists pay closer attention. A weakness that once affected a handful of users can become a safety crisis and a threat to the company’s reputation almost overnight.
 Johanna Glauber is an assistant professor of strategy at IE Business School. Her research examines how firms should organize and govern themselves as they expand their scope. Trained as an engineer, she has a particular interest in how companies prevent product defects as their organization becomes more complex. Akhil Bhardwaj is an associate professor of strategy and organization at the University of Bath. He researches and teaches issues related to executive decision-making, governance, and AI adoption. His prior corporate experience includes working as an engineer and manager at Caterpillar, Inc. and a business analyst advising banks on SOX compliance. Robert Langan is an assistant professor at ESADE Business School, at the Universitat Ramon Llull. His research focuses on corporate governance, executive effectiveness, and interim CEOs. His prior corporate experience includes work in CEO advisory at Spencer Stuart and corporate governance at Credit Suisse Group. Post
